And when she had gone, Socrates sat up on the couch, bent his leg and rubbed it, and said as he rubbed: How strange a thing is what people call pleasure, and how curiously it is related to pain, which might be thought its opposite. The two are never present in a man at the same moment, and yet anyone who pursues one is usually forced to take the other; they are two bodies joined by a single head. And I cannot help thinking that, if Aesop had thought of them, he would have made a fable about God trying to end their quarrel and, when he could not, fastening their heads together. That is why, when one comes, the other follows. I know it from my own experience now: the pain in my leg, caused by the chain, seems to be followed by pleasure.

Very true, said Cebes, laughing gently and speaking in his Boeotian dialect.

Never mind him, Socrates said.
To be sure, Simmias replied.

So, Simmias, before our souls took the form of man they must also have existed apart from any body, and they must have had intelligence.

Then may we not say, Simmias, that if, as we are always repeating, there is an absolute beauty, and goodness, and an absolute essence of all things; and if we refer all our sensations to this, which is now discovered to have existed in our former state, and compare them with it, finding these ideas to be pre-existent and our inborn possession, then our souls must have had a prior existence; but if not, there would be no force in the argument? The proof that these ideas existed before we were born is the same as the proof that our souls existed before we were born; and if the ideas did not, then neither did the souls.

Cebes smiled and answered: Then, Socrates, you must talk us out of our fears — though strictly speaking they are not our fears. There is a child inside us to whom death is a sort of hobgoblin, and we must persuade him too not to be afraid when he is alone in the dark.
Socrates said: Let the voice of the charmer be applied every day, until you have charmed the fear away.
We shall certainly make that search, replied Cebes. And now, if you please, let us go back to the point where our argument digressed.

Those who have chosen the portion of injustice, tyranny and violence will pass into wolves, or into hawks and kites. Where else can we suppose them to go?

Because we may expect them to pass into some gentle, social kind of creature like themselves, such as bees or wasps or ants, or else back into the form of man; and from these just and moderate men may be supposed to spring.

No one is allowed to enter the company of the Gods at his departure unless he has studied philosophy and is entirely pure at that time; only the lover of knowledge may enter. And this is why, Simmias and Cebes, the true votaries of philosophy abstain from all fleshly lusts, hold out against them and refuse to surrender to them. It is not because they fear poverty or the ruin of their families, as lovers of money and the world in general do; nor, as lovers of power and honor do, because they dread the dishonor or disgrace that evil deeds bring.
No, Socrates, that would not suit them, said Cebes.

Certainly not! The soul of a philosopher reasons in quite a different way. It will not ask philosophy to release it only to hand itself over again, once released, to the bondage of pleasures and pains. That would be doing a job only to have it undone, weaving instead of unweaving a Penelope's web. Instead, the soul calms the passions and follows reason. It stays in the contemplation of reason, looking at what is true and divine (which is not a matter of opinion), and it draws its nourishment from that. So it seeks to live in this way while it lives, and after death it hopes to go to what is its own kin and like itself, and to be free of human ills. Never fear, Simmias and Cebes, that a soul nurtured like this, with these pursuits, will be scattered and blown away by the winds when it leaves the body, and be nowhere and nothing.
Socrates answered: You may well be right, my friend, I dare say, but I would like to know in what respect you find the argument insufficient.

Cebes said: I will tell you. My feeling is that the argument stands where it did, and is open to the same objections as before. I am ready to admit that the existence of the soul before it entered the bodily form has been proven very ingeniously and, if I may say so, quite sufficiently. But its existence after death is still, in my judgment, unproven. My objection is not the same as Simmias'. I am not inclined to deny that the soul is stronger and longer-lasting than the body, since I think the soul far excels the body in all such respects. Well then, the argument says to me, why are you still unconvinced? When you see that the weaker thing continues to exist after the man is dead, will you not admit that the longer-lasting thing must also survive for the same length of time? Now I ask you to consider whether my objection, which like Simmias I will put in a figure, carries any weight. My analogy is that of an old weaver who dies. After his death somebody says: He is not dead, he must be alive. See, there is the coat he wove and wore himself, and it remains whole and undecayed. Then he asks someone who does not believe him whether a man lasts longer, or a coat that is in use and being worn. When he is told that a man lasts far longer, he thinks he has proven beyond doubt that the man survives, because the longer-lasting thing is safe if the shorter-lasting thing remains.
Yes, indeed, I said, that is very melancholy.

Cebes said that this part of the argument had impressed him wonderfully, and that his conviction remained absolutely unshaken. Simmias agreed, adding that he could hardly imagine ever coming to think otherwise.
There ought to be, replied Simmias.
But he said: The two propositions, that knowledge is recollection and that the soul is a harmony, are not in harmony with each other. Which of them will you keep?
Or can it do or suffer anything other than what they do or suffer?
I don't follow you, he said.
And if one soul has neither more nor less harmony or discord than another, then it has no more vice or virtue than another, supposing vice is discord and virtue is harmony?

But we have already acknowledged that the soul, being a harmony, can never sound a note against the tensions, relaxations, vibrations and other affections of the strings that compose it; it can only follow them and cannot lead them?

Well, let me tell you something more. There was a time when I thought I understood quite well what greater and less mean. I felt I saw even more clearly that ten is two more than eight, and that two cubits are more than one, because two is the double of one.

Then suppose someone were to say that A is taller than B by a head, and B shorter than A by a head. You would not accept what he said. You would stoutly insist that you mean only this: the greater is greater by, and by reason of, greatness, and the less is less by, and by reason of, smallness. In that way you avoid the danger of saying that the greater is greater and the less less by the measure of the head, which is the same in both. You also avoid the monstrous absurdity of supposing that the greater man is greater by reason of the head, which is small. You would be afraid to draw such a conclusion, would you not?
What you say is most true, said Simmias and Cebes, both speaking at once.

Still, you agree that Simmias does not really exceed Socrates, as the words may seem to imply, because he is Simmias, but because of the size he has. And in the same way, he does not exceed Socrates because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates has smallness when compared with Simmias's greatness?
And if Phaedo exceeds Simmias in size, that is not because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo has greatness relative to Simmias, who is comparatively smaller?

This is why Simmias is called both great and small: he stands in a mean between the two, his greatness surpassing the smallness of one, while the greatness of the other surpasses his smallness. He added, laughing: I am speaking like a book, but I believe that what I am saying is true.
That, replied Cebes, is exactly my notion.
And yet you will surely admit that when snow, as we said before, is exposed to heat, they will not remain snow and heat; but as the heat advances, the snow will either retire or perish?
Yes, of course, he said.
Then whatever the soul possesses, to that it comes bearing life?
In the same way, if the uncooling or warm principle were imperishable, then when cold attacked the fire, the fire would not have perished or been put out, but would have gone away unaffected?
Socrates replied: Yes. Still, everyone will agree that God, the essential form of life, and whatever is immortal will never perish.

I am convinced, Socrates, said Cebes, and I have no further objection. But if my friend Simmias, or anyone else, has something more to say, he had better speak out and not stay silent. I do not know what other occasion he can put it off to, if he wants to say something or hear something said.

The wise and orderly soul follows the straight path and is aware of its surroundings. But the soul that desires the body, as I said before, has long fluttered around the lifeless body and the visible world. After many struggles and much suffering, it is carried off with difficulty and by force by its attendant genius. When it arrives at the place where the other souls are gathered, if it is impure and has done impure deeds, such as foul murders or other crimes akin to these, the works of brothers in crime, then everyone flees from that soul and turns away. No one will be its companion or its guide, and it wanders alone in utter misery until certain times are fulfilled. When they are fulfilled, it is carried irresistibly to the dwelling that fits it. In the same way every pure and just soul, which has passed through life in the company and under the guidance of the gods, has its own proper home.

If I had the art of Glaucus, Simmias, replied Socrates, I would tell you, although I do not know that even the art of Glaucus could prove my tale true, and I could never prove it myself; and even if I could, Simmias, I fear my life would end before the argument was finished. I can, however, describe the shape of the earth and its regions as I conceive them.
